conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is too strong and remains unproven, concluding that current evidence does not establish that a vegetarian diet increases life expectancy compared to eating meat.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is too strong. Current evidence does **not** establish that simply following a vegetarian diet *increases life expectancy* versus eating meat. Most evidence measures *mortality rates*, not actual years of life, and comes from observational cohorts—so dietary differences can be entangled with smoking, body weight, exercise, socioeconomic factors, and overall diet quality.

Evidence is mixed:

* A 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis found vegetarian diets associated with lower **ischaemic-heart-disease mortality**, but **no effect on all-cause mortality** or cerebrovascular mortality; it explicitly rated the evidence as low certainty. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/
* In British vegetarian cohorts, the reported all-cause mortality rate ratio for vegetarians versus nonvegetarians was **1.03 (95% CI 0.95–1.13)**—compatible with no meaningful difference. https://www.dur-a-avaler.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/Mortality+in+British+vegetarians+review+and+preliminary+results+from+EPIC-Oxford.pdf
* Conversely, the Adventist Health Study-2 reported that vegetarian dietary patterns were associated with lower all-cause mortality. But this is still an observational study in a distinctive, generally health-conscious religious cohort, limiting causal conclusions and generalizability. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264/
* A recent prospective-study report notes that relatively few studies have assessed self-identified vegetarianism and mortality and that results have been inconsistent. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s41043-023-00460-9

Thus, vegetarian eating can plausibly improve particular risk factors or disease outcomes, especially when it replaces less-healthful foods, but the broad life-expectancy claim remains unproven.
